assumptions: The paying beachhead is regional waste-ERP, weighbridge, and transport-software vendors with existing cross-border customers, not operators seeking a generic DIWASS portal.
Registered operators can authorize production connectivity and contractually permit the connector to process their shipment records without transferring classification or legal responsibility.
A retained waste-shipment specialist handles domain exceptions and the founder limits the product to integration, conformance, and audit workflows.
Pricing must be justified by avoided vendor engineering, support, and operational interruption rather than by clerical savings alone.
Capital is committed only after a paid conformance pilot, and the founder remains within the stated part-time capacity until repeatable support economics are observed.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Two paid OEM pilots should show signed recurring terms, implementation time, measured reduction in duplicate entry and support incidents, production activation across multiple downstream operators, six-month customer payback, and positive contribution margin after partner share, specialist exceptions, and incident support; a corridor-level count of addressable vendors and operators is also needed.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The mandatory electronic workflow, weak Commission-side validation and reporting, and legacy-system re-keying create a real integration problem. Reframing the offer from another portal to a white-label reliability layer is sound, although commercial APIs, low-cost incumbents, and mature shipment software make the insight useful rather than uniquely proprietary.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Submission failures, stale status, duplicate entry, and audit gaps can interrupt recurring regulated shipments, giving vendors and high-volume operators a plausible reason to pay for embedded reliability. However, the no-fee GUI, low incumbent prices, and the Commission's EUR 1.4 million estimate for total annual administrative savings directly constrain a time-saving pitch; partner willingness to pay for integration and support remains unknown.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Connector minimums, downstream-operator fees, and usage charges can produce recurring revenue and attractive software-like margins if support is bounded, while the proposed initial capital is within the founder's own-capital envelope. The 72% margin, 85% retention, six-month payback, partner share, and route to 600 operators are all unobserved, and security, specialist support, and regulatory incidents could materially reduce owner earnings.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Regional vertical-software vendors serving cross-border waste operators are a coherent, narrow beachhead inside an EU-wide mandatory workflow, and shipment tonnage confirms substantial physical activity. The actual number of suitable vendors, their downstream operator counts, software stacks, and movement frequency are unknown, while physical tonnage does not establish a large connector revenue pool.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Embedding mappings, conformance tests, acknowledgements, and exception handling inside a vendor workflow could establish a useful operational control point. Yet ZEDAL has long workflow experience, Travas and Axians compete at low prices, the Commission exposes a direct path, and channel partners can build or internalize the pattern, so a dominant position is not presently credible.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful connector can reuse technical patterns across additional vendors, countries, shipment procedures, and operator systems, with the Annex VII transition broadening the addressable workflow. Expansion is plausible but depends on how reusable member-state routing and mappings actually are and whether contracts permit cross-customer learning.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Embedded integrations, regression fixtures, mapping libraries, and accumulated failure signatures can lower future implementation cost and create switching friction. The underlying interface is regulated and accessible, data ownership and confidentiality restrict reuse, and both incumbents and partner vendors can reproduce much of the capability, leaving the proposed moat conditional.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Idempotent submission, conformance testing, webhooks, reconciliation, and an auditable exception queue could be materially more convenient than re-keying into a portal for vendors with legacy products. No evidence yet shows superior implementation speed, incident reduction, support cost, or reliability versus incumbents or an internal build, so behavior-changing advantage is unproven.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The May 2026 electronic-exchange requirement is already live, and the Annex VII transition creates another near-term implementation trigger around January 2027. This is genuine regulatory momentum, although mature incumbents are already positioned and the transitional timing reduces first-mover scope.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: White-label distribution through a limited set of regional software vendors could scale downstream access and fits the founder better than repeated direct selling. There is no evidence of partner willingness, sales-cycle length, contract economics, or downstream activation, and the same partners control access and may choose an incumbent or build after learning the integration.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: API integration, state management, data quality, and automated testing fit the founder's skills, commercial software is expressly allowed, and the required capital is technically available. Production access, tenant security, document authentication, changing specifications, urgent incident support, liability allocation, and scarce waste-domain expertise make reliable part-time operation demanding but potentially feasible with a specialist and strict product boundaries.

highest_value_structural_change: Concentrate on one underserved Polish or CEE vendor stack and make the product its contract-bound conformance and support gateway, with an SLA, version-maintenance obligation, and explicit rights to reuse sanitized regression fixtures; price against the vendor's avoided engineering and support burden rather than generic per-shipment administration.
main_structural_strength: The design sells an embedded, recurring reliability layer at the vertical-software control point instead of competing as another operator portal, aligning the regulated workflow with the founder's strongest technical capabilities.
primary_score_limiter: There is no demonstrated vendor-channel demand or contribution economics, and the intended channel partners are also well positioned to use cheap incumbents or internalize the connector.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: A no-fee Commission GUI and mature products from Travas, Axians, and ZEDAL already cover the workflow at low prices, while the Commission estimates only EUR 1.4 million in total annual DIWASS administrative savings.
